title: Reading level chart by grade: Lexile, F&P, DRA, and grade equivalents in one place
summary: One chart for Lexile, Fountas and Pinnell, DRA, and grade equivalents from kindergarten through high school, plus how to use the numbers at home.
body_markdown:
## Why reading levels are confusing (and why that's by design)


Your kid's teacher says she's reading at "level M." The library app says 420L. The curriculum catalog lists "DRA 24." And the standardized test report references "grade equivalent 3.2." They're all describing the same child's reading ability, but none of them seem to agree.


That's because reading level systems were built for different purposes by different organizations. Lexile measures text complexity using word frequency and sentence length. Fountas and Pinnell (F&P) levels reflect a teacher's running record assessment of accuracy, fluency, and comprehension. DRA scores come from a structured one-on-one reading conference. Grade equivalents attempt to map all of it onto a school-year timeline.


None of these systems is "right" or "wrong." They measure overlapping but distinct things. What parents need is a way to translate between them, so when your curriculum says one thing and your kid's assessment says another, you can figure out where they line up.


## The cross-reference chart: Lexile, F&P, DRA, and grade equivalents


The chart below shows approximate correlations across the four most common reading level systems used in the U.S. These are ranges, not exact conversions, because each system measures reading ability differently \[1\].


Approximate ranges by grade. These are not exact conversions.


**Kindergarten:** Lexile BR-190L | F&P A-D | DRA A-4 | Grade equivalent K.0-K.9


**First grade:** Lexile 190L-530L | F&P D-J | DRA 4-18 | Grade equivalent 1.0-1.9


**Second grade:** Lexile 420L-650L | F&P J-M | DRA 18-28 | Grade equivalent 2.0-2.9


**Third grade:** Lexile 520L-820L | F&P M-P | DRA 28-38 | Grade equivalent 3.0-3.9


**Fourth grade:** Lexile 740L-940L | F&P P-T | DRA 38-44 | Grade equivalent 4.0-4.9


**Fifth grade:** Lexile 830L-1010L | F&P T-V | DRA 44-50 | Grade equivalent 5.0-5.9


**Sixth grade:** Lexile 925L-1070L | F&P V-X | DRA 50-60 | Grade equivalent 6.0-6.9


**Seventh grade:** Lexile 970L-1120L | F&P X-Z | DRA 60-70 | Grade equivalent 7.0-7.9


**Eighth grade:** Lexile 1010L-1185L | F&P Z-Z+ | DRA 70-80 | Grade equivalent 8.0-8.9


**High school (ninth through twelfth grade):** Lexile 1050L-1385L | F&P Z+ | DRA 80+ | Grade equivalent 9.0-12.9


Note: Lexile ranges overlap between grades because reading development is not perfectly linear. A strong second grader and an average third grader may share the same Lexile band. That's normal.


## What each system measures (and what it misses)


### Lexile (MetaMetrics)


Lexile measures two things: a reader's ability (from a standardized test) and a text's complexity (from an algorithm analyzing word frequency and sentence length). When the two numbers match, the reader should comprehend about 75% of the text, which is the sweet spot for growth without frustration.


What it misses: Lexile doesn't account for subject knowledge, maturity of content, or engagement. *The Diary of a Wimpy Kid* and a technical manual could share a similar Lexile score, but one will hold a third grader's attention and the other won't. For a deeper look at how Lexile codes work, see our[Lexile levels by grade guide](https://outschool.com/articles/lexile-levels-understand-reading-level) .


### Fountas and Pinnell (F&P) guided reading levels


F&P levels run from A (emergent reader) to Z+ (advanced). Teachers assign levels through running records, where a child reads aloud and the teacher tracks accuracy, self-correction, fluency, and comprehension. It's holistic and teacher-dependent, which makes it more nuanced than a purely algorithmic measure.


What it misses: F&P levels are designed for instructional grouping, not independent reading. A child assessed at level M for instruction can often read level J-K independently and enjoy level N-O as a read-aloud. Parents sometimes mistake the instructional level for a ceiling, which can limit what kids choose to read on their own.


### DRA (Developmental Reading Assessment)


DRA is a one-on-one assessment where a child reads a benchmark book, retells the story, and answers comprehension questions. Scores range from A (pre-reader) to 80 (eighth grade proficiency). Like F&P, it captures more than just decoding, but it requires a trained assessor to administer.


What it misses: DRA scores reflect performance on a specific text on a specific day. A child who's tired, anxious, or uninterested in the assessment book may score lower than their true ability. Homeschool families rarely have access to formal DRA administration, which is one reason the other systems tend to be more practical for home use.


### Grade equivalents


Grade equivalents (like "3.5" meaning "middle of third grade") are the most intuitive system for parents and the most misunderstood by everyone. A grade equivalent of 5.2 on a third grader's test does not mean they should be doing fifth grade work. It means they scored as well as the average fifth grader would on that same third grade test.


What it misses: everything about instructional readiness, content maturity, and social-emotional fit. Grade equivalents are useful as a rough benchmark but dangerous as a placement tool.


When a level number and what you hear at the kitchen table do not match, trust the book they will finish. Then check fluency with a one-minute read of a familiar page. Words correct per minute (WCPM) and a comprehension chat often tell you more than a single letter level.
